ja: だいひゃくじゅうにかい

p.src: In the autumn of the sixteenth year of Yanxi of Shu-Han, General Jiang Wei raised an army of two hundred thousand. He appointed Liao Hua and Zhang Yi as the left and right vanguard commanders, Xiahou Ba as military adviser, and Zhang Ni as commissioner of provisions, then led the great army through Yangping Pass to attack Wei. Jiang Wei consulted Xiahou Ba, saying, “Last time we attempted to take Yong Province, but failed and returned; if we march out again now, the enemy will surely be prepared once more. What wise counsel have you?” Xiahou Ba replied, “Of all the commanderies in Longxi, only Nan’an has abundant money and grain; if we take it first, it will serve well as our base. Our former campaign failed because the Qiang troops did not arrive. This time we should first send someone to rendezvous with the Qiang west of Longshan, then advance through Shiying and march directly from Dongting upon Nan’an.” Jiang Wei was delighted. “Your counsel is excellent!” He accordingly sent Xi Zheng as envoy, bearing gold, pearls, and Shu brocade into Qiang territory to forge an alliance with the Qiang king. Midang, king of the Qiang, accepted the gifts and promptly raised fifty thousand troops. He appointed the Qiang general Ehe Shaoge chief vanguard and marched toward Nan’an.

p.src: When Guo Huai, Left General of Wei, received the report, he sent an urgent memorial to Luoyang. Sima Shi asked his generals, “Who dares go and meet the Shu army?” General Who Supports the State Xu Zhi said, “I am willing to go.” Sima Shi had long known Xu Zhi to be exceptionally valiant and was overjoyed. He appointed Xu Zhi vanguard and Sima Zhao commander-in-chief, then sent them with an army toward Longxi. When the army reached Dongting, it encountered Jiang Wei, and the two armies drew up their battle lines. Wielding a great mountain-cleaving axe, Xu Zhi rode out to challenge them. Liao Hua rode from the Shu ranks to meet him. After only a few bouts, Liao Hua trailed his blade and fled. Zhang Yi spurred forward with leveled spear to meet Xu Zhi; but after another few bouts, he too fled back into formation. Xu Zhi drove his troops forward in a sweeping assault. The Shu army was badly defeated and retreated over thirty li. Sima Zhao also recalled his troops, and each side made camp.

p.src: Jiang Wei consulted Xiahou Ba: “Xu Zhi is exceedingly brave. What stratagem can we use to capture him?” Xiahou Ba replied, “Tomorrow we should feign defeat and overcome him with an ambush.” Jiang Wei said, “Sima Zhao is the son of Zhongda. How could he be ignorant of the art of war? If he sees terrain suited for concealment, he will certainly refuse to pursue. I have seen the Wei army cut our supply route time and again. Now we can use that very tactic to lure them in, and Xu Zhi may be slain.” He summoned Liao Hua and gave him detailed instructions, then summoned Zhang Yi and likewise told him exactly what to do; the two departed at the head of their troops. Meanwhile, he ordered the soldiers to scatter iron caltrops along the road and array many chevaux-de-frise outside the camp, making a show of intending a prolonged stay.

p.src: For several days Xu Zhi led out troops to challenge them, but the Shu army did not emerge. A scout reported to Sima Zhao: “Behind Mount Tielong, the Shu army is transporting provisions with wooden oxen and gliding horses. They intend to hold out for a long campaign while awaiting support from the Qiang troops.” Sima Zhao summoned Xu Zhi and said, “In former campaigns we defeated Shu by cutting its supply route. Now the Shu army is moving grain behind Mount Tielong. Tonight take five thousand troops and sever their supply route; the Shu army will withdraw of its own accord.” Xu Zhi accepted the order. At the first watch he led his troops toward Mount Tielong and, sure enough, saw over two hundred Shu soldiers driving more than a hundred wooden oxen and gliding horses laden with grain and fodder. The Wei troops raised a great shout, and Xu Zhi led the way in blocking them. The Shu troops abandoned all the provisions and fled. Xu Zhi detached half his force to escort the provisions back to camp; he himself led the other half in pursuit. Before they had gone ten li, a barricade of carts blocked the road ahead. Xu Zhi ordered his soldiers to dismount and pull the carts apart, when flames suddenly rose on both sides. Xu Zhi hastily reined about, but in the narrow mountain pass behind him another barricade blocked the road, and flames burst forth there as well. Xu Zhi and his men braved the smoke and flames and spurred their horses through. At the report of a cannon, two forces charged in: Liao Hua from the left and Zhang Yi from the right. After a fierce assault, the Wei troops were utterly defeated. Xu Zhi fought desperately and escaped alone, but both man and horse were exhausted.

p.src: As he fled, another force came charging from ahead. It was Jiang Wei. Xu Zhi was panic-stricken and knew not what to do; Jiang Wei thrust his spear into Xu Zhi’s mount and brought it down. Xu Zhi tumbled from the saddle, and the soldiers hacked him to death with a flurry of blades. The half of Xu Zhi’s force escorting the grain was also captured by Xiahou Ba, and every man surrendered. Xiahou Ba took the Wei soldiers’ armor and horses, had Shu troops don the armor and mount the horses, raised Wei banners, and sent them straight back toward the Wei camp by a minor road. Seeing their own troops return, the Wei soldiers opened the gate and admitted them, whereupon the Shu troops began slaughtering men inside the camp. Sima Zhao was greatly alarmed. As he hurriedly mounted to escape, Liao Hua charged toward him from the front. Unable to advance, Sima Zhao hastily turned back, only for Jiang Wei to arrive with troops by a side road. With every route blocked, Sima Zhao could only draw his troops up Mount Tielong and hold it. The mountain had but one path, while all its other sides were precipitous and difficult to climb; on its summit was only one spring, sufficient for no more than a hundred men to drink. Sima Zhao then had six thousand men under him. Jiang Wei sealed the mountain path, and the spring water was insufficient, leaving men and horses parched with thirst. Sima Zhao looked up to heaven and sighed deeply: “I shall die in this place!” A later poet wrote:

p.src: Secretary Wang Tao remonstrated, “Long ago, when Geng Gong was besieged, he bowed before a well and obtained water from it; why do you not follow his example, General?” Sima Zhao followed his advice. He went to the spring at the summit, bowed twice, and prayed: “I have received an imperial command to repel the Shu army. If I am fated to die, let this sweet spring run dry; I shall cut my own throat and order my entire army to surrender. But if my allotted span and fortune are not yet exhausted, may Heaven swiftly cause the sweet water to well forth and preserve these many lives!” When he had finished praying, water gushed from the spring and could be drawn without exhaustion; thus neither men nor horses perished.

p.src: Meanwhile, Jiang Wei had the Wei troops trapped on the mountain. He said to his generals, “Long ago, at Shangfang Valley, the Prime Minister failed to capture Sima Yi, and I have always bitterly regretted it; but now Sima Zhao will surely be captured by me.”

p.src: Now Guo Huai, hearing that Sima Zhao was trapped atop Mount Tielong, wished to lead troops to his rescue. Chen Tai said, “Jiang Wei has joined forces with the Qiang troops and intends first to take Nan’an. Now that the Qiang troops have arrived, if you withdraw to mount a rescue, they will surely exploit the opening and attack our rear. We should first send someone to feign surrender to the Qiang and contrive our purpose from within. Only after repelling this force can we relieve the siege of Mount Tielong.” Guo Huai agreed. He ordered Chen Tai to lead five thousand troops straight into the Qiang king’s camp. Chen Tai removed his armor, entered, and tearfully bowed, saying, “Guo Huai is arrogant and overbearing and has long desired to kill me, so I have come to surrender. I know every strength and weakness of Guo Huai’s army. Tonight I wish to lead a force to raid his camp. Success will then be assured. When our troops reach the Wei camp, we will have allies within to answer us.” Midang was delighted and ordered Ehe Shaoge to accompany Chen Tai in raiding the Wei camp. Ehe Shaoge ordered Chen Tai’s surrendered troops to remain in the rear and had Chen Tai lead the Qiang troops as the vanguard. At the second watch that night, they reached the Wei camp, whose gates stood wide open. Chen Tai rode in first, alone. As Ehe Shaoge galloped through the gate with leveled spear, he had time for only one cry of anguish before horse and rider plunged into a concealed pit. Chen Tai attacked from the rear and Guo Huai from the left. The Qiang troops fell into chaos and trampled one another; countless men died, and all survivors surrendered. Ehe Shaoge cut his own throat and died. Guo Huai and Chen Tai led their troops straight into the Qiang camp. As King Midang hastily left his tent and mounted, the Wei soldiers captured him alive and brought him before Guo Huai. Guo Huai hurriedly dismounted and personally untied him—another text has “unbound”—then soothed him with kind words: “The court has always regarded you as loyal and righteous. Why, then, have you aided the men of Shu?” Midang was ashamed and acknowledged his guilt. Guo Huai then told Midang, “Lead the vanguard now and go relieve the siege of Mount Tielong. Once the Shu army has been driven back, I shall memorialize the Son of Heaven, and you will surely receive a generous reward.”

p.src: Midang followed his advice and led the Qiang troops in front, with the Wei troops behind, heading straight for Iron Cage Mountain. It was then the third watch of the night, and he first sent a man ahead to inform Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei was delighted and ordered that he be invited in for an audience. Most of the Wei soldiers were mingled among the Qiang ranks. When they reached the Shu camp, Jiang Wei ordered the main body to encamp outside, while Midang led more than a hundred men to the central command tent. Jiang Wei and Xiahou Ba came out to welcome him. Before Midang could speak, the Wei commanders attacked from behind. Jiang Wei was greatly startled and hastily mounted his horse to flee. The Qiang and Wei troops charged in together. The Shu troops scattered in utter disorder, each fleeing for his life. Jiang Wei had no weapon in hand, only a bow and arrows at his waist; in the confusion of his flight, all the arrows fell away, leaving him with an empty quiver. Jiang Wei fled toward the mountains, while Guo Huai pursued him from behind with his troops. Seeing that Jiang Wei was entirely unarmed, Guo Huai spurred his horse and gave chase with leveled spear. As Guo Huai drew near, Jiang Wei feigned drawing his bowstring and made it twang more than ten times in succession. Guo Huai dodged repeatedly, but when no arrows came, he realized that Jiang Wei had none. He therefore hung up his steel spear, took his bow, nocked an arrow, and shot at him. Jiang Wei swiftly dodged the arrow and caught it in passing, then immediately set it to his own bowstring. When Guo Huai had drawn close, Jiang Wei aimed at his face and loosed with all his strength; Guo Huai fell from his horse at the twang of the bowstring. Jiang Wei reined his horse around to kill Guo Huai, but the Wei troops came galloping up. Jiang Wei had no time to finish him off and could only seize Guo Huai's spear before riding away. The Wei soldiers dared not pursue. They hurriedly rescued Guo Huai and carried him back to camp, but after the arrowhead was pulled out, the bleeding would not stop, and he died. Sima Zhao came down from the mountain and led troops in pursuit, but turned back halfway. Xiahou Ba escaped after him and fled together with Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei lost many men and horses and could not rally them along the way, so he returned to Hanzhong. Though he had lost the battle, he had shot Guo Huai dead and slain Xu Zhi, thereby checking Wei's prestige and balancing his fault with his achievements.

p.src: Now Sima Zhao rewarded the Qiang troops and sent them back to their country. He then withdrew his army to Luoyang, where he and his elder brother Sima Shi monopolized the authority of the court, and none of the ministers dared defy them. Whenever Cao Fang, Emperor of Wei, saw Sima Shi enter the court, he trembled without cease. It was as though needles were pricking his back. One day, Cao Fang held court. When he saw Sima Shi enter the hall wearing his sword, he hurriedly descended from the imperial seat to welcome him. Sima Shi laughed and said, “How can there be a rite in which the sovereign welcomes his minister? Your Majesty, pray be at ease.” Presently the ministers reported affairs of state, but Sima Shi decided every matter himself without referring any of them to the Emperor of Wei. After a short while Sima Shi withdrew, striding proudly down from the hall. He rode out of the palace in his carriage, surrounded before and behind by no fewer than several thousand men and horsemen. Cao Fang retired to the rear hall and looked about him; only three men remained at his side: Xiahou Xuan, Minister of Ceremonies; Li Feng, Palace Secretariat Director; and Zhang Ji, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness. Zhang Ji was the father of Empress Zhang and thus Cao Fang's father-in-law. Cao Fang ordered the attendants away and went with the three men to a secret chamber to deliberate. Taking Zhang Ji by the hand, Cao Fang wept and said, “Sima Shi treats me like a child and regards all the officials as mere weeds. Sooner or later, the realm will surely fall into his hands!” When he had finished speaking, he wept bitterly. Li Feng memorialized, “Your Majesty, do not grieve. Though I possess little talent, I am willing, under Your Majesty's enlightened edict, to gather heroes from across the realm and destroy this traitor.” Xiahou Xuan memorialized, “My elder brother Xiahou Ba surrendered to Shu only because he feared that the Sima brothers meant to harm him. If we now destroy these traitors, my brother will surely return. I am an old kinsman of the imperial house; how could I sit by and watch wicked traitors throw the state into disorder? I am willing to join in receiving the edict and campaign against them.” Cao Fang said, “I fear only that we may not succeed.” The three men wept and declared, “We swear to unite our hearts in destroying the traitor and repaying Your Majesty!”

p.src: Cao Fang removed his undershirt embroidered with dragons and phoenixes, bit his fingertip, and wrote a secret edict in blood. Handing it to Zhang Ji, he cautioned him, “My ancestor Emperor Wu executed Dong Cheng because the secret undertaking was not kept confidential. You must proceed with the utmost care and let nothing leak outside.” Li Feng said, “Why does Your Majesty utter such an ill-omened remark? We are not men of Dong Cheng's sort, and how could Sima Shi compare with Your Majesty's ancestor Emperor Wu? Your Majesty, harbor no doubts.” The three men took their leave. At the left side of the Donghua Gate, they came face-to-face with Sima Shi approaching with a sword at his side, followed by several hundred armed men. The three stood by the roadside. Sima Shi asked, “Why are you three so late in leaving court?” Li Feng replied, “His Majesty was reading in the inner court, and we three remained to attend upon his studies.” Sima Shi asked, “What book was he reading?” Li Feng replied, “Books concerning the three dynasties of Xia, Shang, and Zhou.” Sima Shi asked, “On reading that book, what historical matters did His Majesty ask about?” Li Feng replied, “The Son of Heaven asked about Yi Yin's support of Shang and the Duke of Zhou's regency. We all replied, ‘Today, the General-in-Chief Sima is indeed another Yi Yin or Duke of Zhou.’” Sima Shi sneered, “Would you truly compare me to Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou? In your hearts, you really mean that I am Wang Mang or Dong Zhuo!” The three men all said, “We are all men in your service, General. How would we dare think such a thing?” Sima Shi flew into a rage and said, “You are men who flatter only with your mouths! What were you weeping about just now with the Son of Heaven in the secret chamber?” The three replied, “Nothing of the kind occurred.” Sima Shi shouted, “The rims of your eyes are still red with tears! How can you deny it?” Knowing that the affair had already been exposed, Xiahou Xuan raised his voice and cursed, “We wept because your power overawes your sovereign and you intend to usurp the throne!” Sima Shi was furious and ordered his guards to seize Xiahou Xuan. Xiahou Xuan bared his arms, raised his fists, and rushed straight at Sima Shi, but the guards seized him. Sima Shi ordered that each man be searched. On Zhang Ji they found an undershirt embroidered with dragons and phoenixes, bearing words written in blood. The attendants presented it to Sima Shi. Sima Shi examined it and saw that it was a secret imperial edict. The edict read:

You must proceed with the utmost care and let nothing leak outside.”
Li Feng said, “Why does Your Majesty utter such an ill-omened remark?
We are not men of Dong Cheng's sort, and how could Sima Shi compare with Your Majesty's ancestor Emperor Wu?
Your Majesty, harbor no doubts.”
The three men took their leave. At the left side of the Donghua Gate, they came face-to-face with Sima Shi approaching with a sword at his side, followed by several hundred armed men.
The three stood by the roadside.
Sima Shi asked, “Why are you three so late in leaving court?”
Li Feng replied, “His Majesty was reading in the inner court, and we three remained to attend upon his studies.”
Sima Shi asked, “What book was he reading?”
Li Feng replied, “Books concerning the three dynasties of Xia, Shang, and Zhou.”
Sima Shi asked, “On reading that book, what historical matters did His Majesty ask about?”
Li Feng replied, “The Son of Heaven asked about Yi Yin's support of Shang and the Duke of Zhou's regency.
We all replied, ‘Today, the General-in-Chief Sima is indeed another Yi Yin or Duke of Zhou.’”
Sima Shi sneered, “Would you truly compare me to Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou?
In your hearts, you really mean that I am Wang Mang or Dong Zhuo!”
The three men all said, “We are all men in your service, General. How would we dare think such a thing?”
Sima Shi flew into a rage and said, “You are men who flatter only with your mouths!
What were you weeping about just now with the Son of Heaven in the secret chamber?”
The three replied, “Nothing of the kind occurred.”
Sima Shi shouted, “The rims of your eyes are still red with tears! How can you deny it?”
Knowing that the affair had already been exposed, Xiahou Xuan raised his voice and cursed, “We wept because your power overawes your sovereign and you intend to usurp the throne!”
Sima Shi was furious and ordered his guards to seize Xiahou Xuan.
Xiahou Xuan bared his arms, raised his fists, and rushed straight at Sima Shi, but the guards seized him.
Sima Shi ordered that each man be searched. On Zhang Ji they found an undershirt embroidered with dragons and phoenixes, bearing words written in blood.
The attendants presented it to Sima Shi.
Sima Shi examined it and saw that it was a secret imperial edict.
The edict read:

p.src: When Sima Shi had finished reading, he flew into a violent rage and cried, “So you truly were plotting to murder my brother and me! Neither reason nor justice can tolerate this!” He ordered the three men cut in half at the waist in the marketplace and had their three clans exterminated. The three never ceased cursing him. By the time they reached the Eastern Market, all their teeth had been knocked out; each continued to curse indistinctly until he died. Sima Shi went straight into the rear palace. Cao Fang, Emperor of Wei, was just then discussing the matter with Empress Zhang. The Empress said, “There are many eyes and ears in the inner court. If the affair should be exposed, I shall surely be implicated!” While she was speaking, they suddenly saw Sima Shi enter, and the Empress was greatly alarmed. With his hand on his sword, Sima Shi said to Cao Fang, “My father established Your Majesty as sovereign, and his merit and virtue were no less than those of the Duke of Zhou. And in my service to Your Majesty, how do I differ from Yi Yin? Yet now Your Majesty repays kindness with enmity and treats merit as a crime, conspiring with two or three petty ministers to murder my brother and me. Why is this?” Cao Fang said, “I harbored no such intention.” Sima Shi drew the undershirt from his sleeve, threw it on the ground, and said, “Then whose work is this?” Cao Fang was scared out of his wits. Trembling, he replied, “I did it only because others forced me. How would I dare conceive such a thought?” Sima Shi said, “What punishment should be imposed for falsely accusing a great minister of treason?” Cao Fang knelt and pleaded, “I am indeed guilty. I beg the General-in-Chief to forgive me!” Sima Shi said, “Your Majesty, please rise. The laws of the state cannot be set aside.” Then, pointing at Empress Zhang, he said, “She is Zhang Ji's daughter and must by rights be eliminated!” Cao Fang wept bitterly and begged him to spare her, but Sima Shi refused. He ordered his men to drag Empress Zhang away, and inside the Donghua Gate they strangled her with a length of white silk. A later poet wrote:

p.src: The next day, Sima Shi assembled all the ministers and said, “The present sovereign is dissolute and devoid of virtue. He treats actors and courtesans with unseemly familiarity, gives ear to slander, and bars the path of the worthy. His offenses exceed even those of the Prince of Changyi of Han, and he is unfit to rule the realm. I propose, with due observance of the precedents set by Yi Yin and Huo Guang, to establish another sovereign, thereby preserving the state and bringing peace to the realm. What say you?” They all replied, “If the General-in-Chief performs the deeds of Yi Yin and Huo Guang, he will indeed be answering Heaven and complying with the will of the people. Who would dare disobey your command?” Sima Shi then entered Yongning Palace together with the assembled officials and reported the matter to the Empress Dowager. The Empress Dowager said, “Whom does the General-in-Chief intend to establish as sovereign?” Sima Shi replied, “In my judgment, Cao Ju, Prince of Pengcheng, is intelligent, benevolent, and filial, and may fittingly become lord of the realm.” The Empress Dowager said, “The Prince of Pengcheng is my uncle. If he were now established as sovereign, what position would that leave me in? There is now Cao Mao, Duke of Gaogui District, a grandson of Emperor Wen. He is gentle, respectful, and modest, and may be established instead. You senior ministers should consider the matter with a view to the future.” One man memorialized, “The Empress Dowager speaks rightly. He should be established at once.” When they looked, they saw that it was Sima Fu, an elder kinsman of Sima Shi’s clan. Sima Shi then sent an envoy to Yuancheng to summon the Duke of Gaogui District. He asked the Empress Dowager to ascend the Taiji Hall, summoned Cao Fang, and rebuked him: “You have indulged without restraint in debauchery and treated actors and courtesans with unseemly familiarity; you are unfit to inherit the rule of the realm. You shall surrender the imperial seals and ribbons, resume your title as Prince of Qi, and depart at once. You may not enter the court again unless summoned by edict.” Cao Fang wept and bowed before the Empress Dowager, surrendered the imperial regalia, then mounted a prince’s carriage and departed, wailing bitterly. Only a handful of loyal and righteous ministers saw him off with tears in their eyes. A later poet wrote:

p.src: Now Cao Mao, Duke of Gaogui District, styled Yanshi, was a grandson of Emperor Wen and a son of Cao Lin, Prince Ding of Donghai. That day, Sima Shi summoned him by command of the Empress Dowager. The civil and military officials prepared the imperial carriage and went to welcome him with bows outside the Western Side Gate. Cao Mao hastily returned their salutations. Grand Commandant Wang Su said, “Your Majesty should not return their salutations.” Cao Mao replied, “I too am a subject. How could I fail to return their salutations?” The civil and military officials helped Cao Mao into the imperial carriage to enter the palace, but he declined, saying, “I do not know why the Empress Dowager has summoned me. How would I dare ride into the palace in the imperial carriage?” He therefore proceeded on foot to the Eastern Hall of the Taiji Palace. Sima Shi came out to receive him. Cao Mao bowed first, and Sima Shi hurriedly raised him up. After they had exchanged greetings, Cao Mao was led before the Empress Dowager. The Empress Dowager said, “When I saw you in your childhood, you bore the aspect of an emperor. You may now become lord of the realm. You must practice reverence and frugality, restrain expenditure, spread virtue, and exercise benevolence. Do not bring shame upon the late emperor.” Cao Mao repeatedly declined in all humility. Sima Shi ordered the civil and military officials to escort Cao Mao from the Taiji Hall, and that same day he was enthroned as the new sovereign. The sixth year of Jiaping was redesignated the first year of Zhengyuan, a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the realm, and General-in-Chief Sima Shi was granted the yellow battle-ax, the privilege of entering court without hastening his steps, of being addressed without his personal name when presenting affairs, and of wearing a sword in the palace hall. All the civil and military officials received promotions and rewards according to their rank.
